topic: Why embarrassing moments stay in memory (emotional memory)
title: Why Embarrassing Memories Stick Around
voiceover: Why do you still cringe at that embarrassing moment? After an emotional experience, a brain region called the amygdala activates your stress-hormone systems. Neuroscientist James McGaugh argued that this signal helps the brain store the memory more strongly. But a strong memory is not always an accurate one. On September 12, 2001, researchers asked 54 students to record how they heard about the attacks, then retested them up to 32 weeks later. Their memories of the attacks became just as inconsistent as their memories of an everyday event. Yet only for the everyday memories did vividness and belief in accuracy fade. So when a cringe memory feels crystal clear, remember that clarity is not proof of accuracy. Tomorrow: did everyone else notice that moment as much as you think?

description: Why does an embarrassing moment replay in your head for years? Research suggests emotional arousal helps your brain store memories more strongly, but a vivid memory is not necessarily an accurate one. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: McGaugh, J. L. (2004). The amygdala modulates the consolidation of memories of emotionally arousing experiences. Annual Review of Neuroscience, 27, 1-28. Source: Talarico, J. M., & Rubin, D. C. (2003). Confidence, not consistency, characterizes flashbulb memories. Psychological Science, 14(5), 455-461.
accuracy_note: Flashbulb-memory study (Talarico & Rubin 2003) had 54 students at one university. The amygdala works with other brain regions; the video simplifies. McGaugh's account concerns emotional arousal in general, not embarrassment specifically.
